analysis.one_liner: Extends HIPAA-style privacy rules to health data held by apps, wearables, and data brokers.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee reported the bill favorably on July 30, 2026, and it has sat on the Senate calendar since August 4, 2026 without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill extends HIPAA-style privacy, security, and breach-notification rules to health data that federal law currently does not cover — information held by health apps, fitness trackers, wellness devices, and data brokers. Companies would need your written permission before selling, licensing, or marketing your health data, you would gain rights to access, correct, delete, and move your data, and the data could not be used to investigate or punish anyone for seeking or providing health care. Enforcement would fall to the health department and the FTC through civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose health data lives outside HIPAA today: users of period-tracking, fitness, mental health, and telehealth apps, wearable-device owners, and people whose searches and location reveal health interests. They would gain consent rights before their data is sold, rights to access and delete it, protection from data being handed to the government without a warrant or subpoena, and protection from data being used against them for obtaining health care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health apps and wearables

how_it_helps.text: Closes the HIPAA gap: companies outside the health system that decide how health information is used — including data brokers — would have to follow privacy, security, and breach notification standards at least as strong as HIPAA's, within 18 months of enactment.
Requires the individual's written authorization before any sale, licensing, transfer, or marketing of their health data, and lets them revoke that authorization.
Gives individuals enforceable rights to a privacy notice, access, amendment, deletion within 30 days of request, and portability of their data between apps and devices.
Bars companies from collecting or keeping more health data than needed, and from selling or transferring it to any government entity except under a warrant, subpoena, or court order.

Prohibits using or disclosing health data to investigate or impose liability on anyone for seeking, obtaining, providing, or facilitating health care — a protection relevant to reproductive and other contested care.

Tightens de-identification: data could only be stripped of identity through a stricter expert-determination process, recipients must contractually agree never to re-identify it, and re-identification itself becomes a violation carrying civil penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, health and wellness app makers, wearable-device companies, and advertisers that currently buy and sell health-related data would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from unauthorized sale of that data. Health systems and record vendors are mostly already covered by HIPAA and would see little new burden; one section actually lets them charge fees when a patient sends records to a third party the patient chose.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, health apps, and ad tech

drawbacks.text: None of the protections exist until HHS and the FTC write the rules — up to 18 months after enactment — and the real strength of the law would depend on how those agencies draft and enforce them.

The bill gives enforcement to HHS and the FTC through civil penalties and an agreement dividing responsibility between them; it does not give individuals a right to sue violators themselves, so wronged consumers would depend on two federal agencies to act.

When a patient directs their electronic health record to a third party they designate, providers may condition the transfer on that recipient paying fees in advance and accepting binding terms, which could add costs or friction for patients using outside services — though the bill bars this from amounting to unlawful information blocking.

Data already governed by other regimes — financial data under Gramm-Leach-Bliley, substance-use treatment records, student records, regulated research — is carved out of the new definition, leaving those regimes in place rather than strengthening them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real and large: health data held by apps and brokers is among the most sensitive data sold today, and the bill would bring it under consent, minimization, and breach rules at least as strict as HIPAA's. The main weaknesses are structural, not substantive — protections hinge on future rulemaking and on HHS and FTC enforcement rather than private lawsuits, and the fee provision for third-party record transfers modestly shifts costs onto patients' chosen services. On balance, a well-designed privacy upgrade whose practical value depends on vigorous implementation.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate health committee with a substitute amendment and now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for a floor vote that no one has scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on November 4, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which he chairs.

On July 30, 2026, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute — meaning it approved a rewritten version — and on August 4, 2026 Cassidy reported it and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 538.

The rewrite strengthened the original: it added the written-authorization requirement for any sale or marketing of health data, a 30-day deletion right, restrictions on transfers to government, the bar on using health data to investigate people for obtaining care, and a ban on re-identifying de-identified data, while dropping earlier provisions on wellness-data notices and a study on paying patients for their data.
No floor vote has occurred; with the Congress running through January 3, 2027, the bill's fate now depends on Senate leadership finding time for it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet, so no one has gained or lost; if the bill stalls on the calendar, data brokers and health-data sellers keep operating under today's far weaker rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undetermined; data sellers keep the status quo

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and as committee chairman reported it favorably on August 4, 2026 with a substitute amendment that strengthened its privacy protections.

for.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 30, 2026, advancing it to the Senate calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The Republican committee chairman sponsored the bill and one Democratic senator cosponsored it, and the committee advanced it without a recorded vote, so no partisan split is visible in the record yet.

industries.note: The bill names data brokers in its definitions and bars them and any regulated entity from selling, licensing, or transferring health data without the individual's written authorization, or to the government without compulsory process. Their core business of trading health-related data without consent is directly targeted.

industries.industry: Health, wellness, and fitness app and wearable makers
industries.note: Data from step counters, period trackers, symptom checkers, and telehealth apps would suddenly carry HIPAA-grade consent, minimization, deletion, and breach-notification duties. Companies lose the ability to monetize this data freely, though they gain one predictable national standard.

Health-related targeting data — including precise geolocation suggesting someone sought a health service — would require written authorization before any marketing use, cutting off a lucrative data stream.

New rules would govern how much health data AI and machine-learning models may use and require minimum-necessary practices for training data, but developers also gain a clear national framework and standards for privacy-preserving techniques instead of uncertainty.

They are already HIPAA-covered, so the new regime barely touches them, and one section lets them charge advance fees and set binding terms when a patient sends records to a patient-designated third party — a small gain that can add costs for patients using outside services.

analysis.trajectory: A bill reported to the Senate calendar in August of the second year of a Congress rarely gets floor time on its own; unless leadership schedules a vote or it moves by unanimous consent or rides on a larger package, it will likely die when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027 and have to start over next Congress. Its favorable committee report and bipartisan sponsorship give it a plausible, but not strong, path.
